title: Turkey work
subtitle: Looped or cut pile that creates fur, grass, and fluffy surface texture
excerpt: Turkey work builds a dense pile on fabric by forming secured loops of thread that stand proud of the surface. Each loop is held in place by a small anchoring stitch before and after it is formed, so it cannot be pulled out. The loops can be left intact for a curly effect or cut and teased apart to produce a soft, fur-like pile.
sourceNotes: Documented in Dillmont, T. de, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886); Caulfeild, S.F.A. & Saward, B.C., The Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

content.text: Turkey work produces a raised pile of thread loops on the surface of the fabric. Each loop is locked in place by a small securing stitch on either side of it, so the loops cannot slide or pull out. When the loops are cut open and the thread ends are brushed or teased apart, the result is a soft, dense pile that reads as fur, short grass, hair, or any fluffy texture. Rows are always worked from the bottom of the design upward, so each new row of loops sits above the previous one and neither covers it nor flattens it.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton (3 to 6 strands for a full pile), wool thread, or tapestry wool. Thicker threads produce denser, more visible pile. Stranded cotton teases out well after cutting.

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Medium to heavy evenweave, linen, or wool fabric. The fabric needs enough body to support the pile without distorting. Avoid very fine fabrics as the repeated stitching can weaken them.

items.label: Needle
items.value: Chenille needle (size 18 to 22) or tapestry needle for thicker threads. The eye must accommodate the thread comfortably without fraying it.

items.label: Hoop
items.value: A firm hoop or slate frame. The fabric must stay taut throughout so the securing stitches form correctly and the pile stands upright.

content.text: Start at the bottom edge of the area being filled. Bring the needle up at (A) but do not pull the thread fully through. Leave a short tail of about 1 to 2 cm on the surface. This tail will become part of the pile.

Insert the needle at (B), 2 to 3 mm to the right of (A). Bring it back up at (C), which sits between (A) and (B). Pull the thread firmly to form a small securing stitch. This stitch holds the tail down so it cannot pull through to the back.

Bring the needle up at (D), just to the right of (B). Form a loop of thread on the surface by holding a fold of thread down with your thumb to the height you want the finished pile to be (typically 1 to 2 cm for a cut pile; shorter for looped pile). Keep your thumb on the loop.

Insert the needle at (E), 2 to 3 mm to the right of (D), and bring it back up at (F) between (D) and (E). Pull firm. This second securing stitch locks the base of the loop so it cannot pull out. Release your thumb. The loop should stand upright.

Continue across the row: each loop is formed between two securing stitches, stepping 2 to 3 mm to the right each time. Keep the loops a consistent height by using a small piece of card or a matchstick as a gauge to hold each loop over while you stitch. When you reach the end of a row, secure the thread on the back and start the next row directly above the first.
Fill the area row by row, always working upward. If you work downward, the new loops will be covered and flattened by the rows above them.

To finish as cut pile, slide small sharp scissors through the loops and cut across them. Then tease the cut ends apart with the tip of a needle or a soft brush to fluff the pile. Trim with scissors to even the length if needed. To keep looped pile, leave the loops uncut. Looped pile gives a tighter, curlier texture and is useful for tight animal fur or curled grass.

items.symptom: Loops pull out when the thread is tugged
items.cause: The securing stitches were too loose or not pulled firm before moving on.
items.fix: Pull each securing stitch tight enough that it grips the fabric. The stitch should be short (2 to 3 mm) and sit flat against the surface. If a loop pulls out after cutting, the securing stitches on either side of it were not firm.

items.symptom: The pile looks uneven and ragged
items.cause: Loop heights varied because nothing was used to gauge them consistently.
items.fix: Hold each loop over a strip of stiff card or a matchstick of the intended height before stitching it down. Remove the gauge after the securing stitch is in place. Keep the gauge the same throughout the section.

items.symptom: New rows of loops are buried under earlier rows
items.cause: Rows were worked from the top of the design downward.
items.fix: Always start at the bottom of the area and work upward. Each completed row falls forward and downward, leaving the next row above it clear.

items.symptom: The pile is thin and sparse after cutting
items.cause: Too few strands were used, or the rows were spaced too far apart.
items.fix: Work with at least 3 to 4 strands of stranded cotton, or use a thicker thread such as tapestry wool. Space rows no more than 3 to 4 mm apart so the pile is dense enough to cover the fabric.

content.text: Turkey work is used for animal fur, short grass, lamb's fleece, hair, and any area that needs a raised, textured surface. It pairs well with a
outline around the filled area to give it a clean edge, or a
border to define the silhouette of an animal or figure before the pile is trimmed to shape.
